t: A ball rolls across the floor. How do you tell someone exactly what it did?
A ball rolls from here to there. Without showing them, can you say exactly what happened?
A ball crosses a room. To describe it you need three things: where it started, where it stopped, and how long it took.
Motion is change of position over time. Describing it completely requires a reference point, a displacement, and an interval — and the choice of reference point changes the description.
sub: You need to say where it started, where it stopped, and how long it took.
Three numbers: where from, where to, how long. That is a full description of a journey.
Position, displacement, and time interval — the minimum complete description of any motion.
Position relative to a reference, displacement as a vector, and the time interval over which both are measured.

question: You are on a train, holding a ball. The train moves. Is the ball moving?
You hold a ball on a moving train. Is the ball moving?
A ball sits in your hand on a moving train. Is it moving?
A ball is at rest in your reference frame on a moving train. Is it in motion?
options: Yes, it is moving with the train
No, it is sitting still in your hand
Both are true — it depends who is asking
stages.outcome: Both are true — it depends who is asking
note: There is no right answer yet. Pick the one that feels right.
Commit to one before you check. The gap between your guess and the answer is what you will remember.
This is a reference-frame question. Predict before checking — the prediction is what makes the answer stick.
Galilean relativity: the answer depends on the inertial frame. Predict first, then verify.

t: Push the ball. Watch what happens when the ground is rough.
Push the ball with the slider. Try rough ground and smooth ground. Watch what stops it.
goal: Push hard enough to reach the goal.
Find a push that overcomes the friction and reaches the goal.

t: Push the ball to the goal. Work out what friction does before the sim tells you.
Reach the goal. Predict which push–friction combinations will get there before you launch — then check.
goal: Reach the goal. The friction is working against you.
Reach the goal. Determine the minimum push for a given friction coefficient.

t: That thing the ball did — going from here to there — is called motion.
Going from here to there is called motion. How fast you go is called speed.
Motion is change of position over time. Speed is how fast: distance divided by time.
Motion is the change of an object's position with respect to a reference frame over a time interval. Speed is the scalar rate: |Δx|/Δt.
sub: How fast you go is called speed.
Speed is how much ground you cover in each second.
Speed = distance ÷ time. The units are metres per second.
Velocity is the vector form — speed with a direction. The distinction matters as soon as motion turns.

t: When a car brakes, it is just a ball with friction. The same rule tells you when it stops.
A car braking is the same sim with bigger numbers. The friction stops it — and the rule is the same.
Braking distance scales with the square of speed because kinetic energy scales with v². The sim you just ran is the proof.
Highway braking distance follows from F=ma and the work–energy theorem: d = v²/(2μg). The simulation is the same integrator.

q: You hold a ball on a moving train. Is the ball moving?
A ball sits still in your hand on a moving train. Is it moving?
A ball is at rest in your frame on a moving train. Is it in motion?
A ball is stationary relative to you on a train moving at constant velocity. Is the ball in motion?
options: Both are true — it depends who is watching
No, it is sitting still in your hand
Yes, it is moving with the train
why: It depends who is asking. To you, the ball is still. To someone outside, it moves with the train. Both are right.
Both are true. To you the ball is still; to someone on the platform it moves with the train. There is no 'really' moving — only relative to who is watching.
Motion is frame-dependent. In your frame the ball is at rest; in the platform frame it moves at the train's velocity. Galilean relativity: no inertial frame is privileged.
Galilean invariance: the ball is at rest in the train's inertial frame and moving in the platform's. No inertial frame is preferred, so 'really moving' has no absolute meaning.

q: The ball stopped before the goal. What does that tell you?
The ball stopped short of the goal. Why?
In the sim, the ball stopped before reaching the goal. What does that mean?
The integrator halted with x < x_goal. What physical conclusion follows?
options: The push was not strong enough for how rough the ground was
The ball ran out of energy
The goal was too far away
why: Friction is a force that slows things down. When the push is small and the ground is rough, friction wins — and the ball stops. Nothing ran out; a force stopped it.
Friction is a force opposing motion. When friction is larger than the push, the ball decelerates to zero before reaching the goal. It did not 'run out of energy' — a force stopped it.
Friction decelerated the ball to rest. The applied impulse was insufficient to overcome kinetic friction over the required distance. Energy was dissipated as heat, not 'used up'.
The work done by friction (μmg·d) exceeded the initial kinetic energy (½mv²). The ball stopped where the dissipation equalled the imparted energy — a force, not a depletion.
